source_text: Hm... so, with the trace info in hand, what next?  One possibly ideal scenario might be to run Lean in GDB so we could just step through and port the functional behaviour as it runs.

reply_text:
㊥ (what next) I'd rather use GDB for logging than for stepping. Stepping through Lean's startup would mean following about 900 initialization functions one call at a time, which is too slow to port from. What the port has to reproduce is what those calls leave behind: the parser tables, the token table, the attribute and extension registries. So I propose three steps. First, dump that state from real Lean right after initialization. Second, dump the same state from the port at the matching point. Third, list every difference between the two. That list becomes the fix curriculum, known in advance. GDB comes in when one difference needs locating. Shall I start step 1 with codex-5?

🖖 (why a dump rather than stepping) The trace's biggest gap is data. Initialization builds tables that the frontend reads later, and neither callgrind nor stepping shows their contents. A dump shows them directly. Real Lean can read its own registries after initialization, for example the builtin parser categories, the token table, the alias table, the builtin attributes and the list of environment extensions. That gives one canonical TSV per registry. Each difference against the port then becomes one checkable item, like "token `⟨|` missing" or "category `prio` has 3 leading parsers where Lean has 4". This is the "list the fixes in advance from the model" approach you asked for, now with data from Lean itself.

㊫ (where GDB fits) Lean's compiled functions are ordinary C symbols (`l_Lean_Parser_addBuiltinParser` and so on). That means we can set scripted breakpoints on the few registration functions and log each call's arguments in order, calling Lean's own `Name.toString` from GDB to print them. That gives the exact sequence in which Lean registers things. We'd use it when a dump difference depends on order, such as parser priority or which alias wins. The callgrind files already hold caller-to-callee edges, so some of those questions can be answered without GDB.

㊭ (order of work)
1. codex-5 writes a Lean program that runs after initialization and writes canonical TSVs of each registry, with a self-check against facts we already know (the 73 aliases, `namedName` in its category). It's read-only and goes in `lean-wiring`.
2. A Kimi agent gets the port to write the same TSVs at the end of its startup.
3. A diff of the two becomes the fix list, one dispatch per group.

GDB logging is added only for differences the dump can't explain.

previous_reply_acts.text: (tailing callgrind) There's nothing running to tail. Both callgrind runs have already finished, and quickly. The empty file took 6 s under valgrind (23:19:37–43), and `import Lean` took 12 s (23:19:58–23:20:10). Their bg.py logs are `/tmp/futon3c-bg/bg-1790810377973-40.log` and `bg-1790810398922-41.log`, and the raw profiles are `/tmp/envtrace-{empty,import}.cg` and `.cg.1`. So the two-hour limit never came into play. The follow-up job I queued should just come back with "already complete".

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-4
previous_reply_acts.text: (what codex-5 is doing now) codex-5 is correcting how the runs are split, not rerunning them. It split each run where Lean marks the end of initialization (`lean_io_mark_end_initialization`). The second half then also included shutdown code, so it's narrowing "after initialization" to the time spent inside `Lean.Elab.runFrontend`. Its draft table is in `/tmp/envinit-trace-summary.txt`, and its built-in check passes: the parser runs after initialization, and a grind propagator runs only during initialization.
